questions.q:
Two fair dice are thrown. The numbers on them are taken as $\lambda$ and $\mu,$~and a system of linear equations
$x + y + z = 5$

$x + 2y + 3z = \mu$

$x + 3y + \lambdaz = 1$
is constructed. If $p$ is the probability that the system has a unique solution and $q$ is the probability that the system has no solution, then:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
\left|$\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & \lambda\end{cases}$\right| = \lambda - 5$

${Δ}_{1} = \left|$\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & 3 & \mu \\ 3 & \lambda & 1\end{cases}$\right| = 10\lambda + 3\mu - \lambda \mu - 44$

${Δ}_{2} = \left|$\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & 3 & \mu \\ 1 & \lambda & 1\end{cases}$\right| = 5\lambda + \mu - \lambda \mu - 13$

${Δ}_{3} = \left|$\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & 2 & \mu \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{cases}$\right| = - 2\mu + 6$

For unique solution
$\lambda \ne 5, \mu \in { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 }$

$⇒ p = \dfrac{5}{6} \times 1 = \dfrac{5}{6}$
For No Solution
$\lambda = 5, \mu \ne 3$

$⇒ q = \dfrac{1}{6} \times \dfrac{5}{6} = \dfrac{5}{36}$

$

questions.solution:
The unbiased die is thrown& five times such that the product of the outcomes is positive,& then either all outcomes are positive or any two are negative.

Either all outcomes are positive or any two are negative.

Now,

$p = p$~(positive)~$= \dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Required probability

questions.q: A fair die is thrown until $2$ appears. Then the probability, that $2$ appears in even number of throws, is
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let the probability of $2$ appearing in a throw be given by $P \left(2\right)$ and the probability of $2$ not appearing be given by $P \left({2}^{'}\right).

$⇒ $P\left($2\right) = \dfrac{1}{6},$P\left({2}^{'}\right) = $\dfrac{5}{6}$

Now, we want $2$ to appear in {2}^{nd}\text{throw or}{4}^{th}\text{throw or}{6}^{th}\text{throw} . . . \text{and so on}

So, required probability is given by,

P \left(E\right) = $\dfrac{5}{6} \times \dfrac{1}{6} + $\left(\dfrac{5}{6})$3 \times $\dfrac{1}{6} + \left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)5 $\times $\dfrac{1}{6} + . . .$

$⇒ $P\left($E\right) = \dfrac{1}{6} \times \dfrac{56}{1 - \dfrac{25}{36}}$

$⇒ $P\left($E\right) = \dfrac{1}{6} \times \dfrac{56}{1136}$

$⇒ $P\left($E\right) = \dfrac{5}{6} \times \dfrac{36}{11} \times \dfrac{1}{6}$

$⇒ $P\left($E\right) = \dfrac{5}{11}$

questions.q: The minimum number of times one has to toss a fair coin so that the probability of observing at least one head is at least $90%$ is:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let a fair coin is tossed& $n$~times, then
$P ( atleastonehead ) = 1 – P ( alltails )$
$= 1 – \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)n > \dfrac{90}{100}$~(given)
$⇒ {\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}^{n} < 1 - \dfrac{90}{100} = \dfrac{1}{10}$
$⇒ {2}^{n} > 10$
$⇒ n \ge 4$

questions.q:
A random variable $X$ has the following probability distribution:

$X$ $0$ $1$ $2$ $3$ $4$
$P \left(X\right)$ $k$ $2k$ $4k$ $6k$ $8k$

The value of~$P \left(\dfrac{1 < x < 4}${x ≤ 2}\right)$is equal to

$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
To find& $P \left(\dfrac{1 < x < 4}${x ≤ 2}\right)or $P \left(\dfrac{A}{B}\right)

We know that

~P\left(\dfrac{A}{B}\right) = \dfrac{P\left(A \cap B\right)}{P\left(B\right)}

Given

$x$ $0$ $1$ $2$ $3$ $4$
$P \left(x\right)$ $k$ $2k$ $4k$ $6k$ $8k$

$P\left(A\right) = \left\{2, 3\right\}$

$P \left(B\right) = \left\{0, 1, 2\right\}$

P\left($A \cap B\right) = $P\left($x = 2\right)$

$P \left($B\right) = P \left(x = 0\right) + P\left(x = 1\right) + P\left(x = 2\right)$

So $P\left(\dfrac{A}{B}) = \dfrac{P\left(x = 2\right)}{P\left(x = 0\right) + P\left(x = 1\right) + P\left(x = 2\right)}

=\dfrac{4k}{k + 2k + 4k} = \dfrac{4k}{7k} = \dfrac{4}{7}

Hence option~$A& is correct.

$

questions.q:
The random variable& $X$~follows binomial distribution $B ( n, p )$, for which the difference of the mean and the variance is $1$.

If $2P ( X = 2 ) = 3P ( X = 1 )$, then $n^{2}P ( X > 1 )$ is equal to
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given that the difference between the mean and variance is& $1$.

$⇒ np - npq = 1$

$⇒ np ( 1 - q ) = 1$

$⇒ np^{2} = 1$

Also given that,

$⇒ 2P ( X = 2 ) = 3P ( X = 1 )$

$⇒ 2 \cdot C2 n p^{2}q^{n - 2} = 3 \cdot C1 n p \cdot q^{n - 1}$

$⇒ 2 \cdot \dfrac{n \cdot ( n - 1 )}{2} \cdot p = 3 \cdot n \cdot q$

$⇒ ( n - 1 ) p = 3 ( 1 - p )$

$⇒ \left(\dfrac{1}{p2} - 1\right)p = 3 ( 1 - p )$

$⇒ \dfrac{( 1 - p ) ( 1 + p )}{p} = 3 ( 1 - p )$

$⇒ 1 + p = 3p$

$⇒ p = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$∴ n = 4$.

Now,

$n^{2}P ( x > 1 ) = n^{2} ( 1 - P ( x = 1 ) - P ( x = 0 ) )= 16\left(1 - C1 4 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)4 - \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)4\right) = 11$

Hence this is the correct option.

questions.q: An unbiased coin is tossed. If the outcome is a head then a pair of unbiased dice is rolled and the sum of the numbers obtained on them is noted. If the toss of the coin results in tail then a card from a well-shuffled pack of nine cards numbered $1,2, 3, \ldots , 9$ is randomly picked and the number on the card is noted. The probability that the noted number is either $7$ or $8$ is
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let,& $A$~be the event that the noted~number is either~$7$~or~$8 .$

And,~${E}_{1}$~be the event that the toss of coin results in head and~${E}_{2}$~be the event that the toss of coin results in tail.

Then, we have~$P\left({E}_{1}\right) = P\left({E}_{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$

And,~$P\left(A | {E}_{1}\right) =P ($getting the sum of the numbers on the pair of dice as~$7$~or~$8 )$

The total number of cases, when a pair of dice is thrown are~$= 6 \times 6 = 36$~and the cases of getting sum~$7$~or~$8$~are~\left\{\left(1, 6\right), \left(2, 5\right), \left(3, 4\right), \left(4, 3\right), \left(5, 2\right), \left(6, 1\right), \left(2, 6\right), \left(3, 5\right), \left(4, 4\right), \left(5, 3\right), \left(6, 2\right)\right\} = 11$~cases.

$⇒ P\left(A | {E}_{1}\right) = \dfrac{11}{36}$

Similarly,~$P\left(A | {E}_{2}\right) = ($getting the number~$7$~or~$8$~from~the numbers~$1, 2, 3, . . , 9 )$

$⇒ P\left(A | {E}_{2}\right) = \dfrac{2}{9}$

Now, using the total probability theorem, we get

$P\left(A\right) = P \left({E}_{1}\right)P \left($A | {E}_{1}\right) + P \left({E}_{1}\rright)P\left(A | {E}_{2}\right)$

$⇒ P\left(A\right) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{11}{36} + \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{2}{9}$

$⇒ P\left(A\right) = \dfrac{11}{72} + \dfrac{1}{9} = \dfrac{19}{72} .

$

questions.q: In a bolt factory, machines& $A, B$~and~$C$~manufacture respectively~$20 % , 30 %$~and $50 %$~of the total bolts.~Of their output~$3, 4$~and~$2$~percent are respectively defective bolts. A bolt is drawn at random from the product. If the bolt drawn is found the defective then the probability that it is manufactured by the machine~$C$& is&
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let& $X ≡$Event that product is defective, then

$P\left(\dfrac{X}{A}\right) = \dfrac{3}{100}P\left(\dfrac{X}{B}\right) = \dfrac{4}{100}P\left(\dfrac{X}{C}\right) = \dfrac{2}{100}$

Now,

$P\left(\dfrac{C}{X}\right) = \dfrac{P\left(C\right)P\left(\dfrac{X}{C}\right)}{P\left(A\right)P\left(\dfrac{X}{A}\right) + P\left(B\right)P\left(\dfrac{X}{B}\right) + P\left(C\right)P\left(\dfrac{X}{C}\right)}$

$⇒ P\left(\dfrac{C}{X}\right) = \dfrac{\dfrac{50}{100} \times \dfrac{2}{100}}{\dfrac{20}{100} \times \dfrac{3}{100} + \dfrac{30}{100} \times \dfrac{4}{100} + \dfrac{50}{100} \times \dfrac{2}{100}}$

$⇒ P\left(\dfrac{C}{X}\right) = \dfrac{100}{60 + 120 + 100}$

$⇒ P\left(\dfrac{C}{X}\right) = \dfrac{5}{14}$

Hence this is the correct option.

questions.q: In a workshop, there are five machines and the probability of any one of them to be out of service on a day is $\dfrac{1}{4}$ . If the probability that at most two machines will be out of service on the same day is ${\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)}^{3}k,$ then $k$ is equal to
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given $n=5, p=\frac{1}{4}$ and $q=1-p=\frac{3}{4}$

Required probability = when no machine has fault $+$ when one machine has fault $+$ when two machines have fault.

$= C0 5 \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)5 + C1 5 \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)4 + C2 5 \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)2\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)3$

$= \dfrac{243}{1024} + \dfrac{405}{1024} + \dfrac{270}{1024} = \dfrac{918}{1024} = \dfrac{459}{512} = \dfrac{27 \times 17}{64 \times 8}$

$⇒ \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)3 \times k = \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)3 \times \dfrac{17}{8}$

$∴ k = \dfrac{17}{8}$

questions.q: Let& ${E}_{1}, {E}_{2}, {E}_{3}$~be three mutually exclusive events such that~$P\left({E}_{1}\right) = \dfrac{2 + 3p}{6}, P\left({E}_{2}\right) = \dfrac{2 - p}{8}$~and~$P\left({E}_{3}\right) = \dfrac{1 - p}{2}$. If the maximum and minimum values of~$p$~are~${p}_{1}$~and~${p}_{2}$~then~  \left({p}_{1} + {p}_{2}\right)$& is equal to:$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
We know that,

$0 \le P\left({E}_{i}\right) \le 1$for~$i = 1, 2, 3$

$0 \le P\left({E}_{1}\right) \le 1$

$⇒ 0 \le \dfrac{2 + 3P}{6} \le 1$

$⇒ P \in \left[- $\dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{4}{3}\right] . . . . . . . . \left($i\right)$

Now for~$0 ≤ P\left({E}_{2}\right) \le1$

$⇒ 0 \le $\dfrac{2 - P}{8} \le$1$

$⇒ P \in \left[-6, 2\right] . . . . . . . . \left(ii\right)$

Now for~$0 ≤ P\left({E}_{3}\right) \le1$

$⇒ 0 \le $\dfrac{1 - P}{2} \le$1$

$⇒ P \in \left[-$1, 1\right] . . . . . . . \left($iii\right)$

Also,~${E}_{1}$~and~${E}_{2}$~and~${E}_{3}$~are mutually exclusive

P\left({E}_{1}\right) ++P\left({E}_{2}\right) ++P\left({E}_{3}\right) \le$1$

$⇒ 0 ≤ $\dfrac{13}{12} - \dfrac{P}{8} \le$1$

$⇒ P \in $\left[\dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{26}{3}] . . . . . . . . . . . \left(iv\right)$

Now taking intersection of all we get,

\dfrac{2}{3} \leP$≤ 1$

So maximum value~${p}_{1} = 1$~and minimum value~${p}_{2} = $\dfrac{2}{3}

So,~${p}_{1} + {p}_{2} = $\dfrac{5}{3}

$

questions.q: In a game, a man wins Rs. $100$ if he gets $5$ or $6$ on a throw of a fair die and loses Rs. $50$ for getting any other number on the die. If he decides to throw the die either till he gets a five or a six or to a maximum of three throws, then his expected gain/loss (in rupees) is :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Probability of success i.e. getting a& $5$~or~$6 = P\left(s\right) = \dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}$.

So, probability of failure i.e. getting any number other than~$5$~or~$6 = P\left(f\right) = 1 - P\left(s\right) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

Let~$X$~be the amount that a man wins in a maximum of three throws.

So,~$X$~can take values :

Case I : First two throws are~$5$~or~$6$, game stops

$⇒ X = 100 ⇒ P\left(X = 100\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Case II : First throw is other than~$5$~or~$6$~and second and third throws are~$5$~or~$6$, game stops

$⇒ X = 50 ⇒ P\left(X = 50\right) = \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{2}{9}$

Case III : First two throws are other than~$5$~or~$6$~and last throw is~$5$~or~$6$

$⇒ X = 0 ⇒ P\left(X = 0\right) = \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{4}{27}$

Case IV : All three throws are other than~$5$~or~$6$

$⇒ X = - 150 ⇒ P\left(X = - 150\right) = \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{8}{27}$

Therefore, expected gain or loss

$= E\left(X\right) = 100 \times \dfrac{1}{3} + 50 \times \dfrac{2}{9} + 0 \times \dfrac{4}{27} - 150 \times \dfrac{8}{27} = 0$

questions.q: Let ${B}_{i}  \left(i = 1, 2, 3\right)$ be three independent events in a sample space. The probability that only ${B}_{1}$ occur is $\alpha,$~only ${B}_{2}$ occurs is \beta and only ${B}_{3}$ occurs is $\gamma .Let $p$ be the probability that none of the events ${B}_{i}$ occurs and these $4$ probabilities satisfy the equations \left(\alpha -2\beta\right)p = \alpha\beta$and~ \left(\beta --3\gamma\right)p = 2\beta\gamma ($All the probabilities are assumed to lie in the interval  \left \left(0, 1\right)\right) Then $\dfrac{P\left({B}_{1}\right)}{P\left({B}_{3}\right)}$ is equal to______.$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let $P\left({B}_{1}\right) = {p}_{1}, P \left({B}_{2}\right) = {p}_{2},$P \left({B}_{3}\right) = {p}_{3}$

given that~${p}_{1}\left(1 - {p}_{2}\right) \left(1 - {p}_{3}\right) = \alpha \ldots \left(i\right)$

${p}_{2} \left(1 - {p}_{1}\right) \left(1 - {p}_{3}\right) = \beta \ldots \left($ii\right)$

${p}_{3} \left($1 - {p}_{1}\right) \left(1 - {p}_{2}\right) = \gamma \ldots \left(iii\right)$

and~ \left($1 - {p}_{1}\right)\left($1 - {p}_{2}\right)\left(1 - {p}_{3}\right) = p \ldots \left(iv\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{p1}{1 - {p}_{1}} = \dfrac{α}{p}, \dfrac{p2}{1 - {p}_{2}} = \dfrac{β}{p}$~and~$\dfrac{p3}{1 - {p}_{3}} = \dfrac{γ}{p}$

Also~$\beta = \dfrac{\alphap}{\alpha + 2p} = \dfrac{3\gammap}{p - 2\gamma}$

$⇒ \alphap - 2\alpha\gamma ==3\alpha\gamma ++6p\gamma$

$⇒ \alphap - 6p\gamma ==5\alpha\gamma

$⇒ $\dfrac{p1}{1 - {p}_{1}} - \dfrac{6{p}_{3}}{1 - {p}_{3}} = \dfrac{5{p}_{1}{p}_{3}}{\left(1 - {p}_{1}\right)\left(1 - {p}_{3}\right)}

$⇒ {p}_{1} - 6{p}_{3} = 0$

$⇒ $\dfrac{p1}{p3} =$6$
